note.seg: The alternative is given, awkwardly enough, in the following sentence.

note.label: wishes
note.seg: This law is awkwardly expressed if the alternative is the death-penalty. But some alternative price of redemption may perhaps have been accidentally omitted.

note.label: possessor
note.seg: Presumably the man who captured him.

note.label: man
note.seg: Both here and in §22.1, himan is run together, eliminating the ending on the pronoun. Liebermann, Gesetze, 3:30, restores both of these as the accusative hine, and suggests that perhaps originally there was a ~ nasal extension mark over the hi which the copyist overlooked. We might also emend the last phrase þam agende him man healfne agelde, ‘one should pay the owner half for him,’ which grammatically is far preferable. But see the parallel (without the awkward intrusion) in §21; the double accusative construction, however, works better with age than with agelde.

note.label: wants.
note.seg: That is, fine or death. See under ‘Theft’ in Commentary.

Einfänger, regelmässig mit bestohlenem Kläger identisch; vgl. o. 26, 1². Den Eigentümer des Sklaven verstanden Frühere gemäss Hl 1. Aber dieser kann doch nicht vom Gericht auf Staatskosten oder vom Kläger dáfür bezahlt werden, dass er ein gemeinschädliches Wertstück nicht gehörig bewacht hat. Auch Hl 1. 3 lässt ihn neben dessen Auslieferung büssen

The captor, as a rule identical with the robbed plaintiff; cf. above 26, 1². Earlier editors understood the owner of the slave, in accordance with Hl 1. But he can surely not be paid by the court at public expense, or by the plaintiff, for having failed to guard properly a valuable piece of property that was a danger to the community. Hl 1. 3, too, makes him pay compensation in addition to handing the slave over
The word properly means ‘owner’; but, as Liebermann points out, the context here requires that the man who possesses his person at the moment must be meant.

note.label: owner
note.seg: It is not clear what ‘the owner’ refers to here. It seems unlikely that it is the owner of the slave (who should have overseen his property better). Liebermann and Attenborough both assume that it is the man who currently holds the slave in his power. But I think it most likely that the payment goes to the man whose property was stolen.
